title: Perfect and peak state transfer on IBM quantum hardware
abstract: We run continuous-time quantum walks with perfect and peak state transfer on a present-day superconducting quantum processor, IBM Quantum's $156$-qubit Heron device ibm_kingston, deliberately without error correction or error mitigation. Perfect state transfer and its relaxations have been studied extensively in algebraic graph theory, where one can prove exactly which graphs move a quantum state from one vertex to another with probability one (or with the largest probability the graph allows, in the case of peak state transfer), and at what time. Our experiments cover perfect state transfer on the hypercubes $Q_2 = C_4$ and $Q_3$, and on the Hamming-weighted paths $\mathrm{HP}_n$, the equitable-partition quotients of the hypercubes $Q_n$, for $n$ up to $20$; peak state transfer on the $X_n$ family for $n$ up to $11$; and, for comparison, moving the state along a path of qubits by a sequence of SWAP gates.
summary: This paper experimentally tests the phenomenon of Perfect and Peak State Transfer using continuous-time quantum walks on a superconducting quantum processor. By implementing the dynamics derived from the XY Hamiltonian on graph structures like hypercubes, the authors demonstrate state transfer fidelity on current NISQ hardware. It serves as a crucial benchmark, comparing theoretical quantum walk predictions against real-world, noisy quantum computation results.
main_problem: The paper investigates the feasibility of achieving Perfect State Transfer (PST) and Peak State Transfer (peak ST) using continuous-time quantum walks on current superconducting quantum hardware.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated the implementation of PST and peak ST on specific graph families, such as hypercubes and Hamming-weighted paths, using the noisy IBM quantum processor.
method: The continuous-time quantum walk is simulated and executed on the IBM Quantum hardware by transpiling the required time evolution operator, $e^{-itH}$, into native quantum gates.
model_or_system: The system models quantum walks on graphs $G$ (e.g., hypercubes $Q_n$), governed by an XY Hamiltonian, $H_{XY}$. The experiment is performed on the IBM Quantum 156-qubit Heron superconducting processor.
key_observables: The primary observables are the transition probabilities $|U(t)_{v,u}|^2$ between vertices, used to diagnose PST ($|U(t)|=1$) or peak ST (maximizing $|U(t)|$).
important_parameters: The key parameters include the graph structure ($Q_n, HP_n, X_n$), the time $t$ (or $	au$), and the Trotter repetition count $r$ used in the gate approximation.
main_assumptions: The experiments are performed naively on noisy hardware without error correction or mitigation, and the time evolution is approximated using the Suzuki–Trotter formula.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate example graphs ($C_4, HP_7, X_4$) and show the implementation pipeline, detailing the steps from the graph structure to the final measurement circuit on the hardware.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical background of PST/peak ST, details the continuous-time quantum walk Hamiltonian and its mapping to quantum gates, and then presents experimental results across various graph families ($Q_n, HP_n, X_n$) on the IBM hardware, comparing results with noiseless simulations.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it bridges theoretical graph theory results (PST) with the practical limitations and capabilities of near-term quantum hardware, providing a concrete testbed for quantum simulation algorithms.
